## Story-level uncertainties

- Hadith to add later: authenticated reports on the beginning of revelation and on the occasion of these ayat, each with a named grader. None is used in this draft.
- Whether these verses were the first to be revealed is a matter of later tradition; the inventory title says so with the word traditionally. A scholar should decide how the page words this.
- The sense of alaq is for the reviewer; the draft gives a common rendering and the Arabic word.
- Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

## How to review

1. Verses: do the listed ayat really contain what each claim says? Is any claim stronger than its ayat?
2. Pronouns and speakers: where the Arabic names none, does the draft say so?
3. Words with more than one reading: decide how the page words each.
4. Omissions: anything the verses say that readers need and the chapter leaves out?
5. No added facts: no name, number, place, reason, emotion or sequence beyond the ayat; no implied chronology.
6. No depiction of any prophet, angel or jinn.
7. Theology and etiquette: cautious wording about prophets; no verdicts; no legal or medical ruling.
8. Kids mode only restates the claims; nothing frightening or misleading.
9. Lessons are marked as interpretation and are modest; none reads as scripture or a promise.
10. Unknowns and tradition: each 'Named in later tradition' line is accurate and only a label.
11. Titles and honorifics: bare names in the draft; honorifics added at render time.
12. Sign-off goes in the platform review flow (name, version, decision), not in this file.

## 1. The command to read  (`#the-command-to-read`)

Cited ayat: 96:1-5

> **96:1** بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ ٱقْرَأْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ
>
> **96:2** خَلَقَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ
>
> **96:3** ٱقْرَأْ وَرَبُّكَ ٱلْأَكْرَمُ
>
> **96:4** ٱلَّذِى عَلَّمَ بِٱلْقَلَمِ
>
> **96:5** عَلَّمَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ

### Claims

**c1** (96:1): The passage opens with a command to read in the name of the Lord of the one addressed, who created.

**c2** (96:2): God created the human being from an alaq, a word often rendered a clinging thing or a clot.

**c3** (96:3): The command to read is repeated, with the statement that the Lord of the one addressed is the most generous.

**c4** (96:4-5): God is the one who taught by the pen and taught the human being what he did not know.

### One-minute summary

The passage opens with a command to read in the name of the Lord who created [c1]. It says that He created the human being from an alaq [c2], that He is the most generous [c3], and that He taught by the pen and taught the human being what he did not know [c4].

### Complete story

The passage opens with a command to read in the name of the Lord of the one addressed, who created [c1].

It says that God created the human being from an alaq, a word often rendered a clinging thing or a clot [c2]. The command to read is then repeated, with the statement that the Lord of the one addressed is the most generous [c3].

The passage ends by saying that God is the one who taught by the pen and taught the human being what he did not know [c4].

### Deep study

The command to read is given without saying what is to be read [c1]. The passage joins creation [c2], generosity [c3] and teaching by the pen [c4] to one and the same Lord [c1]. The word alaq is kept in Arabic here because it is read in more than one way [c2].

### Kids mode

The passage tells us to read in the name of our Lord, who created [c1]. It says that God taught by the pen [c4]. It says that God taught the human being what he did not know [c4].

### Life lessons (educational interpretation)

Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage ties reading and learning to the name of the Lord who created [c1][c4]. Another is that what a human being comes to know is presented as something God taught [c4].

### What the sources do not establish

- Not established: that these verses are the first revelation. The inventory title calls them traditionally the first; the verses themselves do not say so.
- Not established: when, where or how these words came, who spoke them to the one addressed, or who the one addressed is. The verses name no one.
- Not established: what the one addressed was to read. The verse gives no object.
- The Arabic alaq is read in more than one way; this draft keeps the Arabic word beside a common rendering and decides nothing.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the occasion, the place and the circumstances in which these verses came. None is used in the story texts.
